Family Health

Urinary retention: symptoms, causes, tests and next steps

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Urinary retention means that urine remains in the bladder when it should be able to empty. You may pass a little or a substantial amount and still have urine left behind. Sudden inability to urinate requires emergency care; a gradual problem can be quieter, but it also needs assessment.

What urinary retention means

Acute retention develops suddenly, often when the bladder is full but little or no urine can leave. Chronic retention develops over time: a person can still urinate, but the bladder does not empty completely. It is a problem with emptying, not simply another name for passing urine frequently.

Anyone can be affected. It is more common in older men, especially when prostate enlargement interferes with flow, but women can also develop retention. Age-related risk does not mean that a new urinary problem should be accepted as an inevitable part of getting older.

Untreated retention may contribute to infection, stretching and damage of the bladder, leakage or pressure affecting the kidneys. These are more useful explanations than a vague claim that retained urine simply poisons the body. The risk depends on the degree, duration and cause of the problem.

Sudden retention needs immediate help

You may feel an urgent need to urinate but be unable to do so. The lower abdomen can become swollen, tense or painful as the bladder fills. Do not wait for pain to become severe before seeking emergency medical care.

A clinician may need to drain the bladder promptly with a catheter and investigate why it happened. Drinking large amounts to force urine through, straining repeatedly or waiting overnight is not a safe substitute for assessment. An absence of intense pain does not make a sudden inability to pass urine harmless.

Chronic retention can be less obvious

A slow or interrupted stream, difficulty getting started, passing small amounts repeatedly and feeling the need to go again soon after finishing can all occur. Some people wake several times at night or have persistent lower abdominal or pelvic discomfort.

Others have reduced awareness that the bladder is full, or leak urine without much warning. Overflow leakage can occur when an overfilled bladder does not empty properly. Urgency leakage is a different pattern; the feeling of urgency alone does not identify which problem is present.

There is no single number of daily toilet visits that diagnoses retention. Symptoms can also overlap with other urinary conditions, and some people with chronic retention notice very little. Measuring urine left after urination helps establish what is happening.

How the bladder normally empties

The kidneys produce urine, which travels through the ureters into the bladder. The bladder stores it until it is released through the urethra, the tube leading outside the body. The ureters and urethra are different structures, so the location of any obstruction matters.

Emptying requires coordination. The bladder muscle contracts while the outlet and sphincter muscles allow urine to pass. Bladder-neck mechanisms work largely automatically; the external sphincter and pelvic floor also contribute to voluntary control. Nerves carry messages about fullness and coordinate the change from storing to releasing urine.

Where a prostate is present, it sits below the bladder around part of the urethra. It makes fluid that contributes to semen; it is not the organ that stores urine. Its position means enlargement or inflammation can nevertheless interfere with the urine stream.

Blockage or narrowing of the outlet

An obstruction can partly or completely prevent urine leaving the bladder. Possible causes include scar-related narrowing of the urethra or bladder neck, swelling, a stone at the outlet, a blood clot, a foreign body or a nearby mass pressing on the passage.

Severe constipation can also contribute. A pelvic growth may be noncancerous or cancerous; a mass does not automatically mean cancer. Tight pelvic-floor muscles can interfere with the coordinated relaxation needed for emptying even without a solid object blocking the urethra.

A sudden blockage may cause acute retention, while gradual narrowing may produce a longstanding problem. A kidney or ureter stone does not always cause bladder retention: a blockage higher in the urinary tract can affect urine drainage from the kidney and needs its own assessment.

Medicines can affect emptying

Some medicines reduce bladder contraction or change the signals and muscle tone involved in emptying. Relevant groups can include anticholinergic medicines used for bladder symptoms, antihistamines, decongestants such as pseudoephedrine, some antidepressants or antipsychotics, medicines for Parkinson's disease, muscle relaxants and opioids such as morphine.

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and stimulant medicines, including amphetamines, also appear in medication reviews of possible contributors. This does not mean every medicine in a class causes retention in everyone, or that a prescribed treatment is necessarily the explanation for your symptoms.

Bring the names and doses of prescriptions, cold remedies, sleep aids, supplements and other products, together with any recent changes. The prescriber or pharmacist can assess interactions and alternatives. Do not abruptly stop important treatment without advice, and do not delay emergency care while trying to decide which tablet caused the problem.

Nerve signals and bladder-muscle strength

The bladder may fill without a normal sensation of fullness, fail to contract strongly enough or contract while the outlet does not relax appropriately. These mechanisms can leave urine behind even when there is no mechanical obstruction.

Diabetes-related nerve damage, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, stroke, brain or spinal injury and injuries affecting pelvic nerves are examples of conditions that may be relevant. A vaginal birth can also affect pelvic tissues and nerve function. Having one of these conditions does not establish the cause without an assessment.

A bladder that has been stretched excessively can also lose effective contraction. The investigation therefore considers both the passage through which urine flows and the strength and coordination of the muscles moving it.

After surgery, pregnancy or childbirth

Temporary difficulty emptying can occur after an operation. Anesthesia can reduce the sensation of a full bladder, intravenous fluids increase the amount it must hold, and pain medicines, swelling or changes around the urinary tract can contribute. Joint replacement and spinal surgery are among procedures after which this can be seen.

Risk varies with the operation, anesthesia, medicines and the patient. A percentage reported in one surgical group cannot be used as everyone's personal risk. Tell the team when you last passed urine and report new difficulty promptly instead of waiting until the bladder becomes very uncomfortable.

Pregnancy and birth can also affect emptying. After a delivery, report an inability to urinate, passing only small amounts or a persistent sense of fullness to the maternity team. Reduced sensation can make the problem less painful than expected, so discomfort alone is not a reliable guide.

Prostate enlargement and other prostate conditions

Benign prostatic hyperplasia, often shortened to BPH, is noncancerous prostate enlargement. It can narrow the urethral passage and is an important cause of retention in people with a prostate. Prostate growth becomes more common with age, but enlargement does not mean cancer and does not always produce the same degree of obstruction.

Prostate inflammation and prostate cancer are other conditions a clinician may consider when appropriate. Symptoms alone cannot distinguish all of them. A weak stream should lead to an assessment, not an automatic conclusion that it is ordinary BPH or that it must be malignant.

The history, examination and relevant tests guide management. If a prostate-related problem is found, ask whether the immediate issue is obstruction, inflammation or another mechanism, and how bladder emptying will be rechecked.

Narrowing, foreskin problems and injury

A urethral stricture or narrowing at the urinary opening can affect flow. Injury to the penis, urethra or pelvis may cause swelling or later scar formation. New difficulty urinating after an injury needs prompt assessment, especially if there is blood or significant pain.

A tight foreskin that causes pain or difficulty urinating also deserves examination. A foreskin pulled back behind the glans that becomes trapped and cannot return to its usual position is called paraphimosis; it is an emergency because swelling can compromise blood flow.

Normal foreskin development in babies and young boys is different from a new adult obstruction. A foreskin that does not yet retract is often normal and should never be forced back. A child who cannot urinate needs prompt care rather than attempts to stretch or manipulate the foreskin at home.

Pelvic organ prolapse and other pelvic causes

Pelvic organ prolapse can change support around the bladder and urethra. A cystocele is a bulge of the bladder into the front vaginal wall; a rectocele involves the rectum bulging toward the back vaginal wall. Uterine prolapse means the uterus has descended from its usual position.

These changes do not all cause retention, but substantial prolapse may contribute to difficult emptying. Pressure or a bulge in the vagina, bowel symptoms and the relation of symptoms to standing or straining are useful details to report.

A uterine fibroid or another pelvic mass may also press on nearby structures. Examination helps distinguish a support problem, a mass and another cause. Do not assume that every urinary symptom after pregnancy is simply pelvic-floor weakness or that strengthening exercises are always the right response.

Infection and inflammation

Inflammation can affect the urethra (urethritis), bladder (cystitis) or prostate (prostatitis). Swelling or pain can interfere with normal emptying. Infection is one possible cause of inflammation, but not all inflammation is bacterial.

Balanitis refers to inflammation of the head of the penis and may occur with foreskin inflammation. Vulvovaginitis involves inflammation of the vulva and vagina, rather than just an undefined external part of the vagina. These conditions may cause painful urination or make passing urine difficult and should be assessed according to their cause.

Burning, discharge, redness, fever, chills or new pain helps guide examination and testing. Antibiotics are useful for appropriate bacterial infections, but they are not a universal remedy for retention. A blocked, full bladder may still need drainage while the underlying condition is treated.

What the clinician asks and examines

Expect questions about when the problem began, the stream, urgency, leakage, discomfort and how much urine you pass. Previous surgery or catheter use, bowel habits, medicines, neurologic symptoms and pregnancy or birth history can all be relevant.

The examination may assess the lower abdomen, external genital area, pelvic organs, prostate or rectum, and nerve function as appropriate. The clinician should explain the purpose of an intimate examination and obtain consent; you can ask about a chaperone or a pause.

Making little urine because the kidneys are producing less is different from producing urine that is trapped in a full bladder. Dehydration or kidney illness can reduce output, while retention prevents emptying. Both can be important, and the examination and bladder assessment help separate them.

Measuring retained urine and choosing tests

A postvoid residual measurement shows how much urine is left after you try to urinate. It can be measured by an ultrasound bladder scan or with a catheter. A urine sample may check for infection or other abnormalities, while blood tests can assess kidney function and chemical balance.

Ultrasound can examine the bladder and upper urinary tract. CT or MRI may be useful for a specific concern, such as a stone, mass or spinal problem, but every person does not need every scan. The result should answer a clinical question.

Urodynamic testing examines how urine is stored and released. It may measure flow rate, bladder pressure, capacity or the relationship between pressure and flow. Electromyography assesses muscle responses and coordination around the bladder outlet; these tests provide different information from a simple residual measurement.

Cystoscopy uses a thin viewing instrument to inspect the urethra and bladder for narrowing, stones, inflammation or another structural problem. Ask what each proposed test is intended to find and how its result would change the care plan.

Relieving retention and planning follow-up

The first priority in acute retention is safe relief of the full bladder. After that, treatment depends on the cause. Options may include a supervised medicine adjustment, treatment of infection or constipation, prostate treatment, management of prolapse or a procedure to relieve a narrowing or blockage.

Some people need a catheter temporarily or for longer. If intermittent catheterization is recommended, it requires individual teaching and a clear schedule; an article is not a substitute for that training. Do not insert or remove a catheter without the instructions agreed with your care team.

Before leaving care, ask how bladder emptying will be checked, when the next review is due and what to do if the problem returns. A diary of urine output, symptoms and medicine changes may help follow-up, but it should not postpone urgent treatment.

Other warning signs that should not wait

New difficulty urinating together with worsening back or leg pain, leg weakness, altered feeling around the genitals or buttocks, or a change in bowel control may signal pressure on spinal nerves. Seek emergency assessment; do not wait until all the symptoms are present.

Fever, shaking chills, severe side or back pain, vomiting or feeling seriously unwell alongside urinary symptoms also needs urgent advice. A painful, trapped retracted foreskin needs emergency care. Persistent but less dramatic emptying problems, unexplained leakage or repeated urinary infections should still be reviewed.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Retention may occur even when some urine still passes or leaks.

A postvoid residual measurement helps distinguish symptoms from demonstrable incomplete emptying.

Assessment considers obstruction, muscles, nerves, medicines, operations and birth history.

Treatment should address the cause and include a plan to reassess emptying.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you organize a symptom timeline, a complete medicine list and questions for an appointment. A symptom record cannot measure retained urine or determine which treatment is needed.

When to seek help

Sudden inability to pass urine needs emergency care. New bladder or bowel changes with saddle numbness or worsening back/leg symptoms, or a foreskin trapped behind the glans, also needs emergency assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Passing urine or having leakage does not prove that the bladder empties fully.
  • Acute retention needs immediate help; chronic retention may be painless.
  • Prostate enlargement is only one of several possible causes.
  • Bring prescription and over-the-counter medicine details to the assessment.
  • Ask what caused the problem and how recovery of emptying will be confirmed.

Frequently asked questions

Can I have retention if I still pass urine?

Yes. Chronic retention means the bladder does not empty completely, even though some urine passes. A residual measurement helps assess it.

Can retention be painless?

Yes. Gradual retention or altered bladder sensation may cause little pain. New difficulty emptying should not be ignored because it is comfortable.

Is going more than eight times a day a diagnosis?

No. Frequency has several possible explanations. The pattern, examination and amount left in the bladder are more informative than a fixed visit count.

Does leaking mean the blockage has cleared?

No. An overfilled bladder may leak without emptying effectively. A clinician needs to distinguish overflow from other forms of incontinence.

Does prostate enlargement mean prostate cancer?

No. BPH is noncancerous enlargement. Symptoms still need assessment because inflammation, narrowing and other conditions can produce similar problems.

Should I stop a medicine that might be responsible?

Contact the prescriber or pharmacist for a plan rather than stopping important treatment abruptly. A sudden inability to urinate requires urgent care regardless of the suspected medicine.

Can this happen after an operation or childbirth?

Yes. Changes in sensation, medicines, swelling and pelvic tissue or nerve effects can contribute. Report difficulty promptly to the surgical or maternity team.

Will I need every bladder test listed here?

No. A history, examination and residual measurement guide which additional tests can answer a useful question. CT, MRI, cystoscopy and urodynamics are selected individually.

Should I drink a lot of water to force urine through?

Not as a response to a full bladder that cannot empty. Seek emergency assessment for sudden retention rather than trying to overcome it with large drinks or straining.

Which back symptoms make bladder changes urgent?

New difficulty urinating or loss of control with saddle numbness, worsening back/leg symptoms or leg weakness can signal a spinal nerve emergency. Do not wait for the full combination before seeking help.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
